This equation defines 5 complex numbers which are its roots; but what are they? Can we express them in some kind of “formula”? We know that we can’t express them with radicals, the way we do with equations of degree n = 2 , 3 , 4 . Galois theory precisely shows that (the Galois group of this particular polynomial is the non-solvable group S 5 ). So that’s a first-degree “no” answer to the question. But what about other expressions? Trig functions, logs, etc.? In the paper What is a closed-form number, Tim Chow uses the very same polynomial equation as an example. He then proves that, under the well-known Schanuel conjecture, the roots of this equation (or any other polynomial equation with non-solvable Galois group) are not EL-numbers, which means they cannot be expressed with any of the familiar elementary functions (logs, exponents, trig functions, roots and any combination thereof.) So that’s a second-degree “no” answer: the roots of such equations aren’t EL numbers, which means that they cannot be expressed with formulas consisting of logs, exponents, sines, cosines, arctangents and other familiar functions. Even specific polynomial equations don’t have roots that are expressible in this way, let alone a general formula. But, to be fair, Chow’s result rests on a big, unproven conjecture. It’s possible (though extremely unlikely) that the conjecture is false and that somehow, miraculously, there’s some EL expression for the roots of polynomial equations. So, in that sense, and sticking with EL numbers as the correct universe of “formulas”, the precise answer is “we don’t know”. Finally, the answer may reasonably be “yes” if you allow more flexibility in the concept of “formula”. For example, polynomial equations of degree n = 5 can be solved with the Bring radical, and higher-degree polynomials can be handled with other fancy functions.
